title: What the beans said
translation: Shōkū, the priest of Mount Shosha, had chanted the Lotus Sutra so much that all his senses had been purified, and he could hear what ordinary people can't.

Once, on a journey, he stopped at a hut where someone was boiling beans over a fire of dried bean pods. He heard the beans bubbling in the pot, and what they said was: "You, of all people, our own family, boiling us! How could you be so cruel?"

And this is what he heard the pods answer, crackling in the fire: "Do you think we're doing this because we want to? Burning hurts more than you know. We can't help it. Please don't hold it against us."

{焚|た}かるる{豆|まめ}がらのはらはらと{鳴|な}る{音|おと}は、「わが{心|こころ}よりする{事|こと}かは。
{焼|や}かるるはいかばかり{堪|た}へがたけれども、{力|ちから}なきことなり。
かくな{恨|うら}み{給|たま}ひそ。」とぞ{聞|きこ}えける。
literal: The holy man of Shosha, through the merit of reciting the Lotus Sutra piling up, was a person who had attained the purity of the six senses.

When he stepped into a traveller's hut and heard the sound of beans being boiled over burning bean husks, bubbling 'tsubu tsubu', (the sound) said: 'You, who are no strangers to us, of all people, hatefully boil us and make us suffer bitterly!'
The sound of the burning bean husks crackling 'hara hara' (said): 'Is this something we do of our own will?
Being burned is unbearable beyond measure, but we are powerless.
Please do not resent us like this': so it sounded (to him).

notes.text: Shōkū (died 1007), who founded the Engyōji temple on Mount Shosha, near today's Himeji. He was famous for his devotion to the Lotus Sutra.

The six senses ({六根|ろくこん}): eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body and mind. The Lotus Sutra promises that whoever keeps reciting it gains purified senses, and that purified ears can hear the voices of all beings. That is why he can hear the beans.

The beans and the pods grew on the same plant. The image comes from a famous Chinese poem: Cao Zhi (192–232), ordered by his brother the emperor to compose a poem within seven steps, wrote about beans weeping in the pot over a fire of beanstalks, 'we grew from the same root, why such haste to cook us?'. Kenkō's version gives the stalks a reply.

notes.quote: 辛き目を見するものかな
notes.text: {辛|から}き{目|め}を{見|み}る: 'to have a hard time'. The phrase is still used today. Here it is causative, 見する: 'you make us suffer'.
The sounds: つぶつぶ for the beans bubbling in the pot, はらはら for the dry pods crackling in the fire.

notes.quote: わが心よりする事かは
notes.text: かは: a rhetorical question, 'is it…? (No.)' (see section 137).
な … そ: 'please don't'. The pods are polite even while they burn.
ぞ … ける: 'so it sounded'. {聞|きこ}ゆ: 'to be heard, to sound'. The story ends with the pods' words.
